channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: To the Spencer Street Station
item.description: Compares the muted arrival of the new Southern Aurora express at Spencer Street with the wild 1883 celebrations when Melbourne and Sydney's rail lines first met at Albury, then covers Victoria's new ban on tattooing minors.

item.title: Wild Life in Suburbia
item.description: A Brotherhood of St Laurence survey of a Melbourne housing estate puts hard numbers on Barry Humphries' Mrs Everage caricature, finding suburban Melburnians were overwhelmingly stay-at-home, TV-watching and incurious.

item.title: Keeping up with Carnaby Street
item.description: British fashion designers Roger Nelson and Jean Muir arrive in Melbourne to present the mod Regency look for men, double-breasted with six buttons and floral shirts, and confirm that Melbourne's Lord Henry's Gear store in Russell Street is right up with the latest in Carnaby Street.

item.title: Return of Norm and Edna Everage
item.description: Welcomes Barry Humphries home from London for a nine-night Assembly Hall season, recounting his elaborate public pranks, including the "Ashburton Line" breakfast-in-a-carriage stunt and slices of ham hidden in a David Jones bargain sale.

item.title: The Oyohus of the Pram Belt
item.description: A tour of the outer-suburban display-home craze gripping Melbourne in 1964, from the traffic-snarled exposition villages of East Doncaster to the Brotherhood of St Laurence's grim report on 55,000 families unable to afford decent housing.

item.title: The Monash Story: Keeping Them Down on the Farm
item.description: A portrait of Monash University three years after its unexpectedly early opening, examining its car-dependent Clayton campus, its race to become the world's fastest-growing university, its chronic underfunding, and the outsized personalities shaping its character.

item.title: O, the Opulence of O!
item.description: A behind-the-scenes tour of Reg Ansett's Austarama TV studio at Nunawading, showcasing the opulent new Channel O before its August 1964 launch, with a pointed reminder of Ansett's 1963 promise to show Australians what Australia has to offer.

item.title: You Can't Get Much Lusher
item.description: The Fabulous Lido, a lavish theatre-restaurant in Melbourne's old Savoy building, is about to open, with millionaire ex-dancer David Hamilton McIlwraith pouring half a million pounds into gold mosaic tiles, chandeliers imported from Egypt and long-legged hand-picked showgirls.

item.title: Norm and I Adore Satire and Yoga
item.description: Barry Humphries returns to Melbourne from London, more polished and confident, with a new show at the Comedy Theatre, an updated Mrs Norm Everage who now does yoga and hangs her own pasta on the clothesline, and stories of waiting outside the Savoy in drag to ambush the Prime Minister.

item.title: Loyalty that opens cheque books and office doors
item.description: A review of John McLaren's book 'Our Troubled Schools' examines Melbourne's public-school pecking order, from Geelong Grammar at the top for the landed aristocracy through to junior technical school students at the bottom, and the intolerable dilemma facing parents over where to educate their children.

item.title: One more week
item.description: A Melbourne arts round-up taking in the National Gallery of Victoria's new building and its first temporary exhibition, a Jawaharlal Nehru memorial at Sydney's Australia Square, Brisbane's new Sunday entertainment laws, and filmmaker John Heyer's latest attempt to raise money for an Australian feature film.

item.title: A Marvellous Auction Sale
item.description: A charity auction for Melbourne's Cultural Centre raises funds through improbable lots — LBJ's hat, Patrick White's autographed plays, Dita Cobb's false eyelashes — while the centre itself remains mired in a naming dispute between 'National Gallery and Art Centre of Victoria' and the simpler 'Artorium'.

item.title: Nobody could paint cows better than Scheltema
item.description: A portrait of Melbourne art dealer Julian Sterling and the booming market for Australian paintings, from a $700 Norman Lindsay to $20,000 Drysdales, with a tour of the Heidelberg School artists now fetching serious prices.

item.title: Carping Critics
item.description: Tells how a Fisheries and Wildlife inspector's dawn killing of Ararat's beloved pet carp, Napoleon, provoked a town council uproar and a rueful comment from Premier Bolte, then tracks a beer price rise back to a run on forgotten halfpennies at Melbourne pubs.

item.title: Melbourne v. Sydney: The Love-Hate Feud
item.description: A Melbourne man's affectionate account of the long civic rivalry between Melbourne and Sydney, from Parliament's original seat in Melbourne to the competing airports, opera houses and sporting loyalties that kept the two cities in a state of permanent, mostly enjoyable mutual suspicion.

item.title: Chloe in the Cultural Centre?
item.description: Surveys Melbourne's early-1960s building boom around the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets, from the Flinders Street Station redevelopment to a new cultural centre, and worries aloud that the one thing left untouched, the century-old Young and Jackson's pub and its nude painting of Chloe, might finally be swallowed up.

item.title: A Ruined Week (No Paranoia)
item.description: Surveys a week of civic drama, a State Electricity Commission strike that blacked out television for two nights running, the tabled King's Bridge royal commission report, and the VFL tribunal hearing that suspended Ron Barassi and John Peck on the eve of the finals.

item.title: Henry Bolte's Brilliant Duck
item.description: Premier Henry Bolte stands in as a replacement batsman in a Centenary of International Cricket replay match at the MCG, kitted out in a garish spotted shirt and a learner's L-plate pinned to his back.

item.title: Rosettes in Cream and Gold
item.description: A tour of Victoria's ornate Legislative Council chamber and a survey of its obstructive power over Henry Bolte's government, from a killed Liquor Reform Bill to the enduring mystery of the Legislative Assembly's mace, stolen in 1891 and never recovered.

item.title: Ships That Knock the Rock
item.description: Follows the political stoush over Corsair Rock, the submerged hazard at Port Phillip Heads that holed two coastal freighters within a week, pitting Henry Bolte's government against an opposition demanding it be blasted away, and closes on a wistful case for reviving the old Port Phillip Bay paddle steamers.

item.title: Two Million Babies
item.description: Follows the Melbourne City Council's ballot to crown the city's two-millionth citizen, Sir Rohan Delacombe drawing baby Loretta Johnston's name from a barrel of 1300 contenders, alongside Lord Mayor Maurice Nathan's ceremonial axe-swing on St Kilda Road's aging silver poplars and a survey of migrants arriving on both sides of Britain's colour line.

item.title: £7000 for "Divinely Dressed Ladies"
item.description: The Victoria Racing Club, alarmed by falling attendances, unveils a £7000 best-dressed-racegoer competition for that year's Melbourne Cup carnival, turning the horses into something close to an afterthought.

item.title: What About the Arts — and the Kittens?
item.description: Defends Melbourne's civic pride against a Sydney magazine's charge of drab mediocrity, then traces the theft of a display-only Melbourne Gold Cup replica lent to New Zealand's Tourist Bureau, a farce compounded when the genuine trophy had to travel there in its place for a building opening days later.

item.title: "La Ville de Beauté" (as the French Say)
item.description: Melbourne wins bragging rights as Australia's "Conference City," hosting the World Power Conference's 1000-plus delegates through a whirlwind of interpreters, transistor earphones, and two 1600-guest banquets in the Exhibition Building.

item.title: Football and TV
item.description: Covers Melbourne's fierce row over the VFL's ban on televising the last quarter of League football, then Victoria's new tallest building, the 24-storey Consolidated Zinc, opening almost unnoticed.

item.title: Mr Bolte and the Students
item.description: Profiles David Hirt, the bearded theological student leading Melbourne University's campaign against the hanging of Robert Tait, and the students' months-long standoff with a dismissive Henry Bolte government.

item.title: An Albert Tucker for 2s. a Mile
item.description: Tours the newly opened John Batman motor inn, Robin Boyd's design showcase hung with original Nolans and Tuckers, from its £500,000 build cost down to its black-carpeted penthouse suite.

item.title: Now They Call Him "Satchmo" Bolte
item.description: Traces the Exhibition Building's rise from would-be demolition target to beloved 1963 Trade Fair venue via its riotous 1880s exhibition history, then catches Henry Bolte earning the nickname "Satchmo" over a misquoted Anthony Trollope line about Victorian boasting.

item.title: St Kilda Rd — or Disneyland Modern
item.description: Laments the once-grand St Kilda Road's decline into brash "Disneyland Modern" office architecture, then reports on the inaugural meeting of Melbourne's new Noise Abatement Society, modelled on "America's quietest city," Memphis.

item.title: NSW–Vic: Is Peaceful Co-Existence Possible?
item.description: A tongue-in-cheek peace plan for the Sydney-Melbourne rivalry, sparked by Melbourne's jetport frustrations and a Senate row over an anti-Melbourne pamphlet, complete with a proposed Bolte-Heffron summit in a railway carriage at Albury.
